title: Choice, memory, and progressive disclosure
outcome: Reduce decision effort while keeping useful options discoverable.
useCase: Export dialogs, status menus, and complex settings.
benefits: Makes choices easier without arbitrarily deleting capability.
drawbacks: Disclosure and defaults can hide important options if poorly chosen.
version: Web UX · WCAG 2.2 · principles, not magic formulas
cue: Less uncertainty, not merely fewer buttons.

trace.title: User decision
trace.detail: A menu is a decision problem. Hick–Hyman-style findings relate choice time to uncertainty in controlled tasks. They do not prove that every product should hide options or use exactly a certain number of buttons. Familiarity, grouping, labels, and task frequency matter.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Observe where hesitation comes from: too many choices, unfamiliar labels, fear of consequences, or missing information. These need different repairs.

Compare a grouped menu with a flat one using realistic tasks. Measure completion and wrong selections, not only how quickly someone clicks any option. Faster mistakes are not an improvement.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail: Hiding every option can increase search and memory burden. A default can help but can also cause a silent wrong choice. Do not use a cognitive “law” as a substitute for context.

recallPrompt: Without notes: Reduce decision effort while keeping useful options discoverable. Explain one example and one failure.
